howto.text: Finish Florida's state-approved 63-hour sales associate pre-license course and pass its end-of-course exam.

howto.text: Submit electronic fingerprints through a state-approved vendor for your background check.

howto.text: Pass the 100-question Florida sales associate exam (75% or higher) at a Pearson VUE testing center.

howto.text: Join a licensed Florida broker, such as Adams, Cameron & Co.'s Ormond Beach office, to activate your license and start working.

Ormond Beach is one of the most established and sought-after communities in Volusia County, which makes it a strong place to build a real estate career. Here’s exactly how to get licensed, and what the local market looks like for a new agent.

How do you get a real estate license in Ormond Beach?

You earn a Florida real estate sales associate license, which is valid statewide. There’s no separate Ormond Beach license. The steps: be 18+ with a high school diploma, complete the 63-hour pre-license course, get fingerprinted, apply to the DBPR, pass the state exam (75% to pass), and activate your license under a broker. Most people finish in two to four months. Full detail is in our Florida licensing guide.

Is Ormond Beach a good market for a new real estate agent?

Yes, in a different way than a boomtown. Ormond Beach is established and desirable, with a mix of beachside properties on the barrier island and family neighborhoods on the mainland along the Granada Boulevard corridor. It draws steady relocation and second-home interest. Across Volusia County, roughly 900 homes sell each month at about a $343,000 median, and inventory has risen, giving newer agents more listings to work and sellers who need representation. It’s a relationship market, which rewards an agent who knows the area and stays visible.

Ormond Beach: The Birthplace of Speed and why that heritage matters

In 1902, Ormond Beach became the site of the first organized automobile racing in America, earning the city the official title “Birthplace of Speed.” Henry Flagler, owner of the legendary Ormond Hotel, built the Ormond Garage in 1904 to support the racing events, making it the first gasoline alley before Indianapolis Speedway ever existed. The city hosted world land speed records throughout the 1900s, cementing its place in automotive history. For modern agents, this heritage attracts a particular buyer. Speed enthusiasts, automobile collectors, and buyers drawn to historic character and legacy communities actively seek Ormond Beach. It’s not just beachfront; it’s a town with a story that appeals to buyers looking for identity and substance, not just a transaction. That difference shows up in buyer conversations and often translates into more engaged, serious long-term owners.

Seasonal migration and Ormond’s older, stable buyer base

Ormond Beach has a median age of 53.6 years, reflecting a significant retiree and established-resident population. The city is home to The Casements, the winter estate purchased by John D. Rockefeller in 1914, which exemplifies Ormond’s tradition of attracting affluent seasonal residents. This demographic creates a distinctive market pattern: peak buyer and seller activity runs from late fall through early spring as winter residents arrive and make real estate decisions. Summer can slow, which can reduce competition for new agents willing to stay visible and active year-round. The stable, older demographic also means buyers here tend to be serious about their decisions, often making fewer impulsive moves and actively valuing agents who understand tax efficiency, estate planning implications, and long-term market trends. It’s a buyer base that rewards genuine expertise and relationship-building over hard-sell tactics.

A market divided: oceanfront estates, golf communities, and family neighborhoods

Ormond Beach is not one market, it’s several, and knowing the difference is essential. Oceanfront condominiums and beachfront estates draw a different buyer than the golf course communities inland (like Halifax Plantation and Ormond Hills), which in turn differ from family neighborhoods along the mainland and Granada Boulevard corridor. Single-family homes make up 64 percent of Ormond’s housing stock, but you’ll also work with coastal condominiums, gated communities, and riverfront properties along the Halifax River. Price ranges span from $250,000 starter oceanfront condos to multi-million-dollar golf estates and luxury oceanfront properties. New agents often overlook how much buyer profiles and sales strategies shift across these segments. An oceanfront buyer focuses on views, erosion concerns, and HOA common charges. A golf community buyer prioritizes amenities, course-access deeds, and resort-style living. A family-neighborhood buyer cares about schools and proximity to shopping and services. Each segment requires its own knowledge and vocabulary, and agents who master this segmentation build client bases faster.

Does the brokerage you start with matter?

More than the town you pick. Your license must be held by a broker, and that brokerage decides your training, tools, and support in the make-or-break first year. In an established market like Ormond Beach, a recognized local name carries real weight, and sellers trust it before you say a word.

Why start your real estate career with Adams, Cameron & Co.?

Adams, Cameron & Co. has been the area’s largest brokerage since 1963, with an office right on West Granada Boulevard in Ormond Beach and around 300 agents across Volusia and Flagler County. New agents get in-house marketing at no cost, seven-day non-competing manager support, structured training, and the global Leading Real Estate Companies of the World referral network. That’s the difference between a desk and a real start.
